theme: The song of Moses, redemption celebrated in worship
readingInstruction: Read Exodus 15:1-27. This is the first song in the Bible sung by the whole people of God. Read the first half aloud as a song of praise, and then read the second half as the first test after the song. Notice how quickly the singing is followed by complaining.
settingTheScene: The Red Sea is behind them, and the Egyptians are dead on the shore. For the first time in four hundred years, Israel is free. What does a free people do? They sing. Exodus 15 is the oldest extended poem in the Bible, and it is the model for the way that redemption is celebrated in worship. Moses and the people sing it, and Miriam leads the women in another song. It looks back at what God has done, and forward to what he will do. After the song comes the wilderness, and the first lesson in how fragile their praise can be.
observation: “I will sing to the LORD, for he has triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider he has thrown into the sea” (v. 1).
“The LORD is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation; this is my God, and I will praise him, my father’s God, and I will exalt him” (v. 2).
“The LORD is a man of war; the LORD is his name” (v. 3).
“Who is like you, O LORD, among the gods? Who is like you, majestic in holiness, awesome in glorious deeds, doing wonders?” (v. 11).
“You have led in your steadfast love the people whom you have redeemed; you have guided them by your strength to your holy abode” (v. 13).
The nations will tremble (vv. 14-16), and God will plant his people “on your own mountain, the place, O LORD, which you have made for your abode” (v. 17).
“The LORD will reign forever and ever” (v. 18).
Miriam the prophetess takes a tambourine, and the women follow her with dancing, singing, “Sing to the LORD, for he has triumphed gloriously” (vv. 20-21).
After three days in the wilderness without water, they come to Marah, where the water is bitter, and the people grumble (vv. 22-24).
The LORD shows Moses a tree, which makes the water sweet. He tells Israel, “I am the LORD, your healer” (vv. 25-26). At Elim they find twelve springs and seventy palm trees (v. 27).
interpretation:
The song is organized in three movements. The first (vv. 1-5) is a retelling of the victory at the sea. The second (vv. 6-12) praises God’s power and holiness. The third (vv. 13-18) looks forward to the journey to the land and God’s eternal reign. It is a poem of memory and hope.

The central line is in verse 2: “The LORD is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation.” This verse will be quoted by Isaiah (12:2) and the Psalms (118:14). The word for “salvation” is yeshuah, the root of the name Jesus. The song is already pointing toward a greater salvation. Note too that the song is personal. “My strength…my God.” The people have moved from asking Moses what he has done to them, to saying, “This is my God.”

Verse 11 asks a rhetorical question that has an obvious answer: “Who is like you, O LORD, among the gods?” No one. The exodus is the demonstration that the God of Israel is not just a tribal deity but the Lord of the whole world. And he is “majestic in holiness.” The song does not separate his power from his holiness. The God who defeats Pharaoh is the God whose character is pure.

The third movement is the one that people sometimes overlook. The song looks ahead: “You have led in your steadfast love the people whom you have redeemed.” The tense is past, but the sentence is about the future, because the poet is so certain that God will finish what he has started that he speaks as though it is done. “You will bring them in and plant them.” God’s purpose is a place where he dwells with his people. The final line is a confession that carries the whole Bible forward: “The LORD will reign forever and ever.”

Then comes the cold shower. In three days, the people are grumbling. The song has hardly died away. Marah, the bitter water, is the first test, and the people fail. God does not rebuke them but provides the tree. It is a lesson that he is the one who heals. The promise of verse 26 sets up the whole covenant: if they will listen to the LORD, they will not suffer as Egypt did. God’s grace comes first, and then his commands.
connection: Revelation 15:3 describes the redeemed standing by the sea of glass “and singing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb.” Isaiah 12:2 quotes verse 2. Paul sings the theme in Ephesians 5:19: “singing and making melody to the Lord with your heart.” The tree that made the water sweet has been compared by many to the cross, which turns the bitterness of death into life.
application:
Sing this week. Even if you do not consider yourself a singer, find a hymn or song about what God has done for you, and sing it aloud.

Look at your own wilderness. Where is there a Marah, a place of bitterness? Ask God to show you the tree.

Notice the speed with which gratitude fades. Write down three things God has done for you recently, and thank him for them before the end of the day.
prayerPrompts: Sing or speak to God of what he has done for you, in your own words.
Ask him to heal what is bitter in your life.
Confess how quickly you forget, and ask him to teach you to sing.
